bibliography.abstract: This study examines the joint effects of flight frequency and schedule differentiation on passenger number, airfare, and revenue in the Australian domestic airline market. It distinguishes between two dimensions of scheduling strategies: between-carrier schedule differentiation and within-carrier schedule dispersion. The monthly panel dataset employed comprises 349 carrier-route-specific cross-sectional units, covering 102 oligopolistic domestic routes (51 airport pairs) in Australia for the 2015M1∼2025M6 period (excluding the COVID period 2020M1∼2021M10). The results show that flight frequency has a consistently positive and significant effect on passenger number and revenue. Between-carrier schedule differentiation is found to increase carrier-route-specific passenger demand and support higher airfare, suggesting that temporal differentiation across competitors reduces direct competition and enhances pricing power. In contrast, more clustered within-carrier scheduling increases passenger attraction by improving service convenience, although its effect on airfare is generally insignificant. To summarise, the empirical findings indicate that a strategy combining higher frequency, greater differentiation relative to competitors, and more concentrated within-carrier scheduling is most conducive to route revenue generation.
bibliography.title: Flight Frequency, Schedule Differentiation, and Route Revenue: Evidence for Competition and Scheduling Policy

en.caveats: The analysis is restricted to oligopolistic domestic routes within a single national market, which may limit how well these scheduling dynamics generalize to highly competitive international markets or different regulatory environments.
en.what: This study analyzes how flight frequency, between-carrier schedule differentiation, and within-carrier schedule dispersion jointly affect passenger volume, airfares, and route revenue. Using a monthly panel dataset of 349 carrier-route units across 102 oligopolistic domestic routes in Australia from January 2015 to June 2025 (excluding the COVID-19 period), the analysis reveals that higher flight frequency consistently boosts passengers and revenue. It also finds that spreading schedules apart from competitors increases demand and airfares, while clustering a single carrier's own flights increases passenger volume without significantly affecting fares.
en.why: The findings demonstrate that temporal scheduling strategies directly influence market power and service convenience, proving that airlines can maximize revenue by combining high flight frequencies with schedules that are clustered internally but differentiated from competitors.
